Evidence within the corpus directly supports the claim that scanned PDFs can weaken citation quality:

- [NL-006-S03] states that a scanned PDF consists of flat page images; if uploaded without OCR, the parser extracts zero text, and OCR failures such as blur, low resolution, or complex layouts directly cause broken citations where TutorChat cannot link to the exact paragraph.
- [NL-006-S04] lists "Format Limitation" as a root cause of missing citations: when an answer is retrieved from a low-resolution scanned PDF, the layout parser cannot determine the exact page or section ID. It also instructs inspectors to check OCR logs for missed page boundaries when the source is a scanned PDF.
- [NL-011-S05] reports that the remaining citation tickets in May and June 2026 are "almost entirely linked to scanned, image-only PDFs," for which TutorChat struggles to establish citation anchors and often links back to the start of the file instead of the specific page.
- [NL-018-S04] documents that for scanned, image-only PDFs, citation mapping still fails: the citation either points to page one of a large document, such as a 150-page code blue response document, or no citation link is generated at all.
- [NL-021-S02] notes that scanned PDFs without an embedded text layer cause TutorChat either to return answers with no source citations because it cannot find text offsets, or to point to the entire document (e.g., page 1 of a 250-page PDF) rather than a specific section.
- [NL-021-S05] proposes flagging scanned, image-only files at upload because ingesting them without OCR "may result in poor citation quality," and gives an example of a scanned PDF with only 45% citation confidence.
- [NL-028-S03] explains that if a question is based on low-quality scanned PDFs, the system may struggle to generate page-specific citations due to OCR limitations.
